title: What is your actual experience with AI handling all the code for more complex games?
author: prois99
selftext:
Hello,

I feel bad for making another post, but it is so hard to get a practical opinion on this. Everywhere I read that coding has been commoditized, that devs do not code etc. Yes ok, not typing code is one thing, but the other thing is architecting and desining the systems. People say they do not write code anymore, but then don´t tell you the rest of the equation, and that is how much technical hand holding they must give to the AI, and how much they still need to design the actual systems.

This is something I want to ask those of you, who are trying to push AI to the limit. Do you feel like we really get along by just blindly vide coding, or have you reached a point, where for AI the codebase became problematic, or too expensive to manage and you had to refactor?

Here we see a lot of cool lookig snippets, but not finished games, I suppose we could find people trying to push it to the limits and giving us actual practical insights.  


Thanks :)

comments.author: cousinned
comments.body: I've never touched code in my life and probably never will. I have taken the rules of a tabletop RPG that I've been running and am migrating the entire entire campaign into a video-game like 3D space (think Baldur's Gate). The way I deal with not coding is just asking other agents to audit the code, write up a report, and send it to the main coding agent for further review. It's all gone well so far at least, but my first real playtest is next week so maybe this will all come crashing down like a house of cards.

replies.author: caesium23
replies.body:
The capabilities of frontier models are a moving target of course, but my experience using the last few versions of Sonnet and Opus have been that they can code just about anything, but that doesn't mean they'll code it _well_. They code just good enough that you can treat it like a magic black box until you're a good way into a complicated project... And then you're going to start running into problems.

You ask for changes that, as a dev, you _know_ should be simple, and it only changes in one place, or breaks something unrelated, or the agent actually pushes back because of how much work it would be. You start asking questions and learn that what it built is just a janky ball of mud and spaghetti code.

It wrote a ton of tests, but they aren't checking the things that actually matter; single responsibilities are scattered across dozens of shallow modules; common helpers are duplicated every single place they're needed. Changes, improvements, and routine maintenance become increasingly painful, and eventually all progress comes to a screeching halt for a couple weeks while you talk through the problems and get it to refactor a large chunk of what it built.

Or you can handhold it through planning how to build every new feature. It takes more time upfront, but it means a lot less refactoring later. Though, which one actually results in less total time would be hard to measure objectively.

comments.author: ImCallingYouOutOnBS
comments.body:
Personally, I believe your code architecture is VERY important for the sustainability of your game. 

I use AI agents, but I also created a custom framework where my agents work on different sections of the code, use versioning, and follow the architectural principles it set.

I have a custom made engine/framework, a custom game editor for the project, heavy documentation and an inhouse wiki, all my agents have multiple .md files for learning, I created a phone app so that I can work on the game from the go, using my laptop as a server when I'm away from home to access my framework, etc. 

If you're making a 1 and done game, you might not need all that, but a games modding community is what can keep it going for years, so my game is setup architecturally so that it's easier to mod, than it is to rip and reupload, and I ensured code readability and steam workshop support from the jump.

This is my hobby, and I admire the creators of dwarf fortress for sticking with one game, and trying to perfect it over years. I'm applying that same principle to mine

comments.author: Seboklarus133
comments.body:
Yes, I hit that wall. I'm not a programmer, and my first approach was pure vibe coding. It worked great until the game got big – everything was in one huge file, and every new feature broke two old ones. The AI kept re-fixing the same bugs and it got slow and expensive.  
What saved it was a full rebuild: split into small modules, one job per file, and the game content (texts, numbers, quests) moved out of the code into data files. In my second game the main file went from about 4000 lines down to under 300 after the rebuild. Then automatic tests – a script that plays the whole game from start to the final boss and takes screenshots of every window, so the AI checks itself after every change.  
So no, it's not blind. I don't write code, but I do the "architect" part: I decide how the game should work, I ask ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini to compare approaches before anything gets built, and I test everything myself. The AI is the builder, not the designer.  
And it does get you to a real game – mine already has 5 of 7 story books, bosses, a village, seasons and a soundtrack, and it's out on itch.io. The last two books are coming, and I'll keep updating it after that. Happy to share the link if anyone wants to see it.

comments.author: FragmentedHeap
comments.body:
I built a whole engine from scratch, I had some rules. 

* All modular, many crates, many repos
* All webgpu using the same pinned binaries
* All capi libraries, (dlls etc)
* Cross platform

I used a research phase, pulling in academic papers, thesises, etc into a concrete plan for building the whole engine and every piece of it. 

Text rendering, webgpu, wasm, windowing, input, sound, ui, ui layout, and on and on. 

Let ai plan breaking it down into its base modules and repos, 

Then I started reviewing that plan and what it was going to make and how many repositories it was going to have and how many crates and how many copi dlls etc 

And then I iterated on that plan until I had everything split out the way I thought it should be. 

And then I let it eat for weeks, many resets, fable 5.2, opus 5.5, google carbon now too, 

When stronger artificial intelligence models come out I do another pass and I go over and look for bugs and do code reviews and then do you fix iterations constantly moving the core engine components to stronger versions. 

And to give it a great chance of success as set up a custom build server for it, it uses gitea on my home lab, and I have 3 build servers, I gave it ssh to all of them and command line to kick off cicd builds and monitor and watch them. 

It has tests on 3 operating systems. 

It does work, reviews, tests locally on windows and wsl2, then kicks off the cicd and tests on Linux windows and mac on my servers. 

Then it publishes everything to my nexus repo and I can go play with it in csharp. 

I designed it in rust, but it builds csharp apis for all of it so I can use everything in csharp. 

The engines in rust babd unmanaged, csharp is more of an orchestrator. 

Currently I have a mtsdf text rebdering engine that renders text in shaders and can render 40k characters in 5 ms or less, still tweaking it. 

And I have a 2d ui engine that can do ui with css and markup without a browser.

I haven't looked at any of the code, I just do more and More AI passes, constantly improving it. 

Currently one of the phases I'm in is to have artificial intelligence make jigs and then try to reproduce and test everything and then compare images and performance benchmarks and try to find issues and memory leaks and things like that. 

But I've done that so many times now it's running pretty good and I'm not finding a lot of places to optimize it.

Once this gets good enough I'll move it to git hub and I'll open source it, and ill hook up ai reviews, so that when people use artificial intelligence to contribute to it I can use everybody else's compute to contribute towards the code base, by having strong AI automatically review pull requests and decide what's good and what's not and then pulling it into branches that I can review. 

That's how a lot of popular projects run now.

The key to having artificial intelligence work on incredibly complex things like this is to modularize the crap out of it.  You need it to be broken down into its smallest components so that the context is only limited to that component. 

Because this framework is already much bigger than will fit in a 1 million context window, it's almost a million lines of code... 

It was a lot more than that but I just did a pass that reduced it by a lot

The text rendering engine is not a small thing it was a massive undertaking and one I'm very passionate about.  And it also includes a complete text rendering engine that's been optimized to be able to work on text files up to a terabyte in size.  It has its own engine and it fully supports Unicode 18 and utf8.  It supports multiple languages including Japanese kanji.  I put many weeks worth of AI computes into making it.  And fed it a whole bunch of academic papers.  I spent more time optimizing that than anything else in the engine. 

Because I'm on a mission to make text look amazing in video games and especially on OLED monitors.

I now  have an engine where you can render text on a billboard in 3D and you can walk around and walk up to it and the text automatically scales and looks really good. 

I can render user interfaces on anything, even water.

I don't write code anymore, I programmed for like 30 years of my life so I can read code...  But I don't think I've manually written a line of code in almost a year.

comments.author: VesperQuest
comments.body:
If you don't manually review you'll be lulled into a false sense of "wow this is amazing" if you have good architecture and standards/ai reviewers in place.

Then it'll start saying things in passing that make you realize a lot of wild things still slipped through the cracks. So wild, in fact, that you'll still say "wow this is amazing".

Manual review is still important depending on what you're doing.  I'm still trying to solve this but opus LOVES to write tests that are either checking that the code does in fact do X and breaks under X being different (but not that the behavior breaks if something else changes). It also loves to write tests AND guards in the code such as "I'll make a guard that stops the server from booting if anything ever tries to make X exist again" if you don't make rules for that.

But in my experience (which truthfully isn't much, I have been a low level SWE since early 2013 but haven't been employed as a SWE that entire time.. have worked on some very cool projects with military robotics and networking) the main thing to really look for in user-facing performance-critical code that absolutely can't be implemented poorly, it always tries to take the easy/lazy route.  Perfect example: yesterday I was working on a system that I planned/sketched out for a few hours thinking I had accounted for every edge case.. because why would someone ever do the obviously wrong things? Gave Claude the draft (opus 5.5 on high) in plan mode, admittedly I didn't look at the plan so this is completely on me and it gave me the most beautifully "wow this is amazing" implementation I've ever seen: every server tick, it re-walked a large (20-50 entries) list of statuses on every connected user to check every single one for expiration. My draft said to use dirty flags and keep separate cache buckets so a status could say exactly when it was due if it got flagged dirty by the system that actually handles those statuses.

-pprof profile for 17,500 mock users with 50 statuses each against a 100ms server tick budget:

Claude's implementation: 1.7s/tick for just this system with 27% of total CPU going to GC on an M5 Max, roughly 950Mb/tick of garbage.

My implementation after corrections: 250 microseconds/tick, 0 allocations on the hot path.

comments.author: Mrbuttshaman
comments.body: You can 100% vibe code a game, but you can't blindly do it.  You really need to be very detailed in what you want.  For me, I eventually created a few skills.  Interface design, game design, etc.  They often function as questionnaires that the AI asks me before running off on its own.  They might even ask for reference pictures or for me to generate a game-bible for it with example styles in it.  Then I have it create a game design document based on that which I review and edit as necessary.  Once that is done, I have it break the project out into milestones.  I have it make the first milestone and make sure that works.  If the game is complex, I have it build each system independently and test that each system works the way I would expect individually.  I have it create a debug menu basically where I can launch into any scene and test it.  Its funny it actually taught me a lot about why these things exist in regular game design as well.  Anyway, once that works, then I weave one segment together(like a town in an RPG game)  make sure I can go to the shops, buy things, talk to people, etc.  If the game has an overworld, I test that, make sure the encounters work correctly, that everything resolves correctly at the end of an encounter, etc.  The big thing is to define your rules and expectations, the LLMs are actually pretty insane at actually making these things work as long as you define what you actually want.

comments.author: DullBody7200
comments.body:
I’m completely new to this, with no previous game development experience, so these are just my thoughts after three weeks of experimenting.

The biggest thing I’ve learnt is how much it helps to work through the game design before getting into the coding. That includes the rules, mechanics, maths, art style, the first ten minutes of gameplay, the repeatable gameplay loop and what will make people want to come back.

I used a combination of my own ideas and AI to put together ten detailed documents, plus an overall game design document. A lot of this came from looking closely at a game I enjoyed and knew well, then thinking through how its different systems might have been designed and built.

I went into quite a lot of detail on the player journey. For example, what happens when someone opens the game for the first time? What are their first few clicks? What should they understand and achieve in the first ten minutes? Then I considered the returning player: how do they load their game, remember where they left off and know what to do next?

I fed those documents into ChatGPT to develop concept artwork, giving it a clear foundation for the maps, characters, furniture and other assets.

From there, I passed everything to Claude and asked it to analyse the design from a game development perspective. I now have agents covering project management, workflow, critique, bug hunting and coding, coordinated by the project manager.

The project manager breaks the work into manageable phases. The agents work through a phase, then I playtest the result to see what works and what needs changing. If the visuals need more work, I take in-game screenshots, use ChatGPT to explore improvements, then give those reference images back to Claude to guide the next iteration.

I also asked for a testing mode that lets me access all the features, along with in-game tools for moving and adjusting objects. That makes it much easier to test things and tweak the layout myself.

There’s probably plenty more I could add or improve, but I’m still learning. That’s the approach I’ve worked out so far.

I do have a bit of a background in projects/user journeys and flows just in a completely different sector 

You may event want to go into gherkin style user stories 

(Given when then) That describes actual behavior 

E.g. 
As a new player, I want to name my character so that I can personalise my experience

Given I am creating a new character
When I enter a name that meets the naming rules
    And I confirm my choice
Then the name is saved against my character
    And I continue to the next step

And so on..

My game has been 100% ai coded I have no code experience
